title: Hardness of 6-coloring 3-colorable graphs
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction \(R\) from Boolean \(3\)-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every \(3\)-CNF formula \(F\),
\[
F\text{ is satisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))\leq3,
\qquad
F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))>6?
\]
Equivalently, is the promise decision problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? This is the previously approved gap-decision formulation of the six-colouring hardness question.
definitions:
A Boolean \(3\)-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals. A literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variables and clause lists are explicitly encoded with binary indices and fixed delimiters; repeated literals and clauses are allowed. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false. Let \(L\) be the complete encoding length.

The reduction is one deterministic multitape Turing machine. On every valid formula it outputs one graph \(G=R(F)\) on a labeled vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), allowing \(n=0\). Encode \(n\) by an explicit unary size header and then list unordered pairs of distinct binary vertex indices as edges, without repeated edges. Thus isolated vertices are included explicitly in the input size and the graph is not a succinct exponentially large object. There are fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the entire computation, including writing the graph, takes at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit operations. There are no random bits, advice or oracle calls. Malformed formulas may be rejected. The graph need not come with any colouring, satisfying assignment or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring of a graph is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(k\), with \(\chi\) of the empty graph defined as zero. For \(k\geq1\), \(K_k\) is the loopless complete graph on \([k]\). A graph homomorphism maps vertices to vertices and sends each edge to an edge, so a proper \(k\)-colouring is exactly a homomorphism to \(K_k\).

The promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) requires YES on graphs with \(\chi(G)\leq3\) and NO on graphs with \(\chi(G)>6\). Graphs of chromatic number four, five or six lie outside the promise; a decision algorithm may answer either way on them. The reduction itself must send every satisfiable formula to the YES region and every unsatisfiable formula to the NO region, so its valid outputs never lie in this middle region. It is a many-one reduction: it produces a single instance and does not query a colouring oracle.

The two reduction implications must hold without a Unique Games, Label Cover, or other unproved hypothesis. NP-hardness here denotes the existence of this unconditional reduction; it is not itself the assertion that the problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. Since Boolean \(3\)-SAT is NP-complete, the displayed reduction is equivalent to the standard deterministic many-one NP-hardness requirement for all NP languages.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction exists, or a proof in Lean that no such reduction exists. A positive answer must specify the construction, prove its uniform polynomial bit complexity and verify both chromatic-number implications for every input formula. Hardness only under an unproved conjecture, a reduction with weaker completeness or soundness, or hardness for a different pair of palettes does not settle this target.

A negative answer must rule out all deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions satisfying the two implications. In particular, a polynomial-time algorithm for the promise problem alone does not unconditionally prove nonexistence of the reduction: combining both would imply \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\). If \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\), a SAT decider could itself construct such a reduction by returning \(K_3\) or \(K_7\) according to satisfiability. Failure of one algebraic gadget construction, inability to find a particular polymorphism, or a finite list of unsuccessful reductions is insufficient for the negative answer.
why: The three-versus-six gap is a concrete fixed-template question in approximate colouring and promise constraint satisfaction. An established reduction would supply a fundamental obstruction to algorithms producing six-colour solutions on promised three-colourable inputs; the newly claimed all-constant result directly addresses this target.

importance.reason: A widely recognized frontier example for promise constraint satisfaction, explicitly posed beyond the known five-colour hardness. Kept separately from the all-constant algorithm question because it asks for an individually significant fixed-template reduction.

progress.text: The algebraic PCSP framework proves the three-versus-five gap as a case of its k-versus-(2k−1) hardness theorem.
Brandts and Živný explicitly pose the six-colouring question in the opening paragraph.
The new SDP-based algorithm improves a growing-palette guarantee while its introduction still records five-colour hardness as the known unconditional constant-palette frontier.
Fei–Minzer–Wang claim the three-versus-k promise-gap hardness for every fixed k in Corollary1.7, including k=6. Full-proof verification of this new preprint remains outstanding in the present review.

context_blocks.text: A promise of three-colourability guarantees that a small partition into independent sets exists but does not reveal it. Allowing six colours relaxes the requested output. The associated decision gap separates graphs admitting three colours from graphs that do not admit even six. This is a small fixed-template promise CSP with no growing palette parameter.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove hardness for distinguishing \(k\)-colourable graphs from graphs not colourable with \(2k-1\) colours, for every \(k\geq3\). At \(k=3\), the result gives a gap from three to five colours. Its NO-instances may still be six-colourable, so the theorem does not imply the three-versus-six gap.

The algebraic PCSP framework relates the available reductions to operations that preserve the promised constraint relations, called polymorphisms. The source demonstrates the strength of this approach with the five-colour theorem and explains that moving to larger palettes requires additional analysis. A limitation of one reduction family does not by itself show that the requested polynomial-time reduction cannot exist.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 theorem reports a polynomial-time algorithm using \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours on an \(n\)-vertex three-colourable graph. Their introduction still identifies five colours as the unconditional hardness frontier in its account. A growing-palette algorithm supplies neither a six-colouring algorithm nor a reduction proving hardness at six colours.

A deterministic polynomial-time six-colouring search algorithm on three-colourable inputs would yield a decision algorithm for this gap: run it with a polynomial time cutoff and check whether its output is a proper six-colouring. Every YES-instance would be accepted, while no NO-instance could pass the check. This one-way implication explains the relevance to search without identifying all possible notions of search hardness with the chosen decision reduction.

The separate question of whether some fixed constant palette allows polynomial-time colouring has a different quantifier. Hardness at six colours would not exclude an algorithm using seven, one hundred or another fixed number. Likewise, logarithmically many colours eventually exceed every fixed palette, so that algorithmic target is distinct from this hardness threshold.

The14September2026 preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game hardness theorem. Its Corollary1.7 explicitly gives the three-versus-k decision gap for every fixed k; taking k=6 would answer the present question affirmatively. This is an exact target match, not merely search hardness or an almost-satisfiable completeness statement. The full proof has not been independently verified in this review, so the result is recorded as a claimed resolution.

sentences: The target is an unconditional polynomial-time reduction that maps satisfiable formulas to three-colourable graphs and unsatisfiable formulas to graphs requiring more than six colours.
Graphs needing four, five or six colours are outside the promise and cannot be valid outputs of the reduction.
Known unconditional hardness at five colours does not automatically extend to six.
A14September2026 preprint claims the required gap for every fixed larger palette, but its complete proof has not been independently verified in this review.
An accepted answer proves existence or nonexistence of the full reduction in Lean.
